title: Operation Cincar: The Washington Agreement's First Military Dividend
sources: ICTY Prlic et al. Trial Judgment (IT-04-74-T)
content:
Seven months after the Washington Agreement ended the Croat-Bosniak war and created the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the strategic consequences of that diplomatic settlement found their first significant military expression in the mountains of western Bosnia. In early November 1994, ARBiH and HVO forces launched Operation Cincar, with the ARBiH 7th Corps conducting the main attack from the northeast, targeting VRS positions around the town of Kupres — a small but strategically important junction sitting at over one thousand metres elevation on the plateau between the Vrbas and Cetina river valleys.

Kupres had been under VRS control since the early weeks of the war. In April 1992, the town's mixed Serb and Croat population had become one of the conflict's first casualties when JNA and Serb paramilitary forces seized the area, driving out the Croat inhabitants. The town's elevation and its position at the intersection of routes linking VRS-held territory in the Krajina with central Bosnia gave it a significance disproportionate to its small population. Control of Kupres meant control of a road network that connected Donji Vakuf, Bugojno, and the upper Vrbas valley — arteries the VRS relied upon for lateral movement between its western and central fronts.

The Federation forces that attacked Kupres in November 1994 were qualitatively different from those that had fought the Croat-Bosniak war the previous year. The Washington Agreement had freed HVO units from the central Bosnian front and enabled coordination with ARBiH formations, allowing concentration of force. Croatian Army involvement in the operation — the extent of which remains debated — may have provided additional artillery and logistical support, though specific HV unit participation at Kupres in 1994 is not well documented (unlike the clearly attested HV role in Operations Summer 95 and Storm the following year).

The fighting for Kupres was intense. The terrain favoured the defender — high elevation, limited approach routes, and winter conditions that restricted manoeuvre. VRS forces contested the advance but were outnumbered and, critically, unable to reinforce the garrison adequately. The Belgrade embargo, imposed three months earlier, had begun to constrain VRS logistics, and the Bosnian Serb military was simultaneously managing threats on multiple fronts, including the crisis developing around Bihac. Kupres fell in early November 1994.

The capture of Kupres carried consequences beyond the immediate tactical gain. VRS supply routes through western Bosnia were now threatened by HVO forces holding the high ground. The operation demonstrated that the Federation alliance was not merely a diplomatic arrangement but a military reality capable of producing coordinated offensive action against VRS positions. For the VRS command, which had grown accustomed to fighting opponents who were either outgunned, isolated, or divided, the emergence of a unified and externally supported adversary on its western flank represented a strategic shift.

Operation Cincar was also a preview. The combined ARBiH-HVO capability demonstrated at Kupres would be applied on a far larger scale the following year in Operations Flash and Storm in Croatia, and in the coordinated Federation offensives in western Bosnia during September and October 1995 that helped create the territorial conditions for the Dayton Agreement. The professional military planning, the integration of artillery and manoeuvre forces, and the willingness to sustain casualties in mountainous terrain all pointed toward a force that was preparing for decisive operations rather than static defense.

For the people of Kupres — both the Croats who had been expelled in 1992 and the Serb residents who now fled — the operation meant another cycle of displacement in a war defined by the violent reshuffling of populations across contested territory.
